claim: Type II topoisomerases modulate chromosome supercoiling, condensation, and catenation by moving one double-stranded DNA segment through a transient break in a second duplex.
source: Type II topoisomerases modulate chromosome supercoiling, condensation, and catenation by moving one double-stranded DNA segment through a transient break in a second duplex.
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism of type II topoisomerases supported by extensive prior research in the field.

claim: At physiological enzyme concentrations, eukaryotic type IIA topoisomerases (topo IIs) readily coalesce into condensed bodies.
source: Here, we show that at physiological enzyme concentrations, eukaryotic type IIA topoisomerases (topo IIs) readily coalesce into condensed bodies.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy data showing puncta formation at physiological concentrations (Figure 2C, Figure 6).

claim: DNA stimulates condensation of topo II and fluidizes these assemblies to impart liquid-like behavior.
source: DNA stimulates condensation and fluidizes these assemblies to impart liquid-like behavior.
evidence: FRAP experiments show that DNA increases the mobile fraction of protein in condensates (Figure 3B, Figure 4E-F).

claim: Condensation induces both budding yeast and human topo IIs to switch from DNA unlinking to active DNA catenation.
source: Condensation induces both budding yeast and human topo IIs to switch from DNA unlinking to active DNA catenation, and depends on an unstructured C-terminal region, the loss of which leads to high levels of knotting and reduced catenation.
evidence: Activity assays show that under condensate-forming conditions, topo II produces catenated DNA networks that remain in the well of agarose gels (Figure 5A, Figure 6D-E).

claim: The switch from DNA unlinking to catenation depends on an unstructured C-terminal region.
source: Condensation induces both budding yeast and human topo IIs to switch from DNA unlinking to active DNA catenation, and depends on an unstructured C-terminal region, the loss of which leads to high levels of knotting and reduced catenation.
evidence: Deletion of the CTD prevents condensation and shifts activity to knotting rather than catenation (Figure 5C-D).

claim: Loss of the C-terminal region leads to high levels of knotting and reduced catenation.
source: Condensation induces both budding yeast and human topo IIs to switch from DNA unlinking to active DNA catenation, and depends on an unstructured C-terminal region, the loss of which leads to high levels of knotting and reduced catenation.
evidence: ScTop2ΔCTD produces extensive DNA knotting as shown by gel electrophoresis after nicking (Figure 5D).

claim: Type II topoisomerases resolve DNA supercoiling and entanglements that arise naturally from the action of transcription, replication, and repair machineries on chromosomes.
source: Type II topoisomerases resolve DNA supercoiling and entanglements that arise naturally from the action of transcription, replication, and repair machineries on chromosomes (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Type II topoisomerases modulate DNA topology by an ATP-dependent strand passage mechanism.
source: Enzymes of this family modulate DNA topology by an ATP-dependent strand passage mechanism in which one duplex segment is physically passed through a transient, protein-mediated break in a second double-stranded DNA (Brown and Cozzarelli, 1979; Wang, 1998).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citations to Brown and Cozzarelli, 1979 and Wang, 1998.

claim: Two classes of type II topoisomerases have been identified: type IIA and type IIB.
source: Two classes of type II topoisomerases have been identified to date: type IIA, which comprise proteins such as eukaryotic topo II, prokaryotic topo IV and DNA gyrase, and type IIB, which include two isoforms, topo VI and topo VIII, which are found in plants, archaeal organisms, and some viruses (Forterre et al., 2007).
evidence: This classification is supported by citation to Forterre et al., 2007.

claim: DNA gyrase adds negative supercoils to DNA.
source: Apart from gyrase, which adds negative supercoils to DNA (Gellert et al., 1976), all other type II topoisomerases tend to 'simplify' DNA topology – for example, relaxing supercoiled DNA, untying DNA knots, or unlinking catenated loops – in accord with a lowering of the torsional or entropic energy of the system (Rybenkov et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gellert et al., 1976.

claim: All type II topoisomerases except gyrase tend to simplify DNA topology in accord with lowering torsional or entropic energy.
source: Apart from gyrase, which adds negative supercoils to DNA (Gellert et al., 1976), all other type II topoisomerases tend to 'simplify' DNA topology – for example, relaxing supercoiled DNA, untying DNA knots, or unlinking catenated loops – in accord with a lowering of the torsional or entropic energy of the system (Rybenkov et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rybenkov et al., 1997.

claim: Type II topoisomerases can actively form complicated DNA structures such as knots and catenanes, depending on conditions.
source: However, type II topoisomerases can also actively form complicated DNA structures such as knots and catenanes, depending on conditions.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the following sentences describing specific conditions.

claim: Knotted DNAs can be formed in vitro using high concentrations of bacteriophage T4 topo II.
source: For example, knotted DNAs can be formed in vitro using high concentrations of bacteriophage T4 topo II (Wasserman and Cozzarelli, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wasserman and Cozzarelli, 1991.

claim: Catenated DNAs can be generated by type II topoisomerases through the addition of proteinaceous or chemical DNA condensing agents.
source: Catenated DNAs can be generated by type II topoisomerases through the addition of proteinaceous or chemical DNA condensing agents (Krasnow and Cozzarelli, 1982; Riou et al., 1985; Tse et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krasnow and Cozzarelli, 1982; Riou et al., 1985; Tse et al., 1984.

claim: Both DNA knots and catenanes can be created in vitro when high concentrations of eukaryotic topo II are present relative to DNA.
source: Both DNA knots and catenanes can be created in vitro when high concentrations of eukaryotic topo II are present relative to DNA (Hsieh, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsieh, 1983.

claim: The relative concentrations of both DNA and enzyme play a significant role in controlling whether type II topoisomerases selectively remove linkages or add linkages.
source: Overall, the relative concentrations of both DNA and enzyme appear to play a significant role in controlling whether type II topoisomerases selectively remove linkages (simplifying DNA topology) or add linkages (complicating topology).
evidence: This is inferred from the preceding examples and citations.

claim: Human topo II is present at low-to-sub micromolar levels in cells.
source: In cells, DNA is maintained at a high concentration (millimolar base pairs) compared to that of the topoisomerase (e.g., human topo II is present at low-to-sub micromolar levels in cells [Padget et al., 2000]), yet the enzyme is capable of altering its catalytic output to suit specific needs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Padget et al., 2000.

claim: During transcription and replication, positive DNA supercoils generated by RNA polymerases or replisomes are recognized and relaxed by type II topoisomerases to prevent stalling.
source: For example, during transcription and replication, positive DNA supercoils generated by RNA polymerases or replisomes are recognized and relaxed by type II topoisomerases to prevent stalling (Liu and Wang, 1987; Lockshon and Morris, 1983; Pruss, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu and Wang, 1987; Lockshon and Morris, 1983; Pruss, 1985.

claim: Following replication, interlinked chromosomes are decatenated by enzymes like topo II and topo IV to prevent DNA breaks.
source: Similarly, following replication, interlinked chromosomes are decatenated by enzymes like topo II and topo IV to prevent DNA breaks (Cebrián et al., 2015; Hiasa and Marians, 1996; Lucas et al., 2001; Peter et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cebrián et al., 2015; Hiasa and Marians, 1996; Lucas et al., 2001; Peter et al., 1998.

claim: Topo II can create knots in regions with high transcriptional activity.
source: However, some type II topoisomerases can also create knots, such as the action of topo II in regions with high transcriptional activity (Valdés et al., 2018), a function that can locally compact DNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Valdés et al., 2018.

claim: Topo II has been proposed to actively catenate DNA as a means of promoting chromosome condensation and/or cohesion.
source: Topo II has also been proposed to actively catenate DNA as a means of promoting chromosome condensation and/or cohesion (Anderson and Roberge, 1996; Bauer et al., 2012; Farr et al., 2014; Ishida et al., 1994; Tavormina et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson and Roberge, 1996; Bauer et al., 2012; Farr et al., 2014; Ishida et al., 1994; Tavormina et al., 2002.

claim: Vertebrates express two different topo II isoforms – Top2α and Top2β – that have specific cellular roles.
source: One clue to understanding the disparate topological outcomes mediated by type II topoisomerases can be found in vertebrates, which express two different topo II isoforms – Top2α and Top2β – that have specific cellular roles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate topo II isoforms.

claim: Top2α is essential in dividing cells where it assists in cell-cycle functions such as chromosome condensation and segregation.
source: Top2α is essential in dividing cells where it assists in cell-cycle functions such as chromosome condensation and segregation (Gonzalez et al., 2011; Johnson et al., 2009; Nielsen et al., 2020; Samejima et al., 2012; Spence et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gonzalez et al., 2011; Johnson et al., 2009; Nielsen et al., 2020; Samejima et al., 2012; Spence et al., 2007.

claim: Top2β plays a role in supporting transcriptional initiation.
source: By comparison, Top2β plays a role in supporting transcriptional initiation (Edmond et al., 2017; Haffner et al., 2010; Lyu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Edmond et al., 2017; Haffner et al., 2010; Lyu et al., 2006.

claim: Functional differences between Top2α and Top2β derive in part from a variable, intrinsically disordered C-terminal domain (CTD) appended to an evolutionarily conserved catalytic core.
source: Evidence suggests that functional differences between Top2α and Top2β derive in part from a variable, intrinsically disordered C-terminal domain (CTD) appended to an evolutionarily conserved catalytic core (Linka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Linka et al., 2007.

claim: The CTD of topo II is subject to extensive post-translational modifications.
source: The CTD is subject to extensive post-translational modifications (Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2019; Bedez et al., 2018; Cardenas et al., 1992; Grozav et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2000), has been shown to mediate interactions with different partner proteins (Lane et al., 2013; Nakano et al., 1996; Niimi et al., 2001; Yamane et al., 1997) and, specifically for Top2α, appears to help localize the enzyme to specialized chromosomal regions such as centromeres (Andersen et al., 2002; Pandey et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2019; Bedez et al., 2018; Cardenas et al., 1992; Grozav et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2000.

claim: The CTD has been shown to mediate interactions with different partner proteins.
source: The CTD is subject to extensive post-translational modifications (Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2019; Bedez et al., 2018; Cardenas et al., 1992; Grozav et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2000), has been shown to mediate interactions with different partner proteins (Lane et al., 2013; Nakano et al., 1996; Niimi et al., 2001; Yamane et al., 1997) and, specifically for Top2α, appears to help localize the enzyme to specialized chromosomal regions such as centromeres (Andersen et al., 2002; Pandey et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lane et al., 2013; Nakano et al., 1996; Niimi et al., 2001; Yamane et al., 1997.

claim: The CTD of Top2α appears to help localize the enzyme to specialized chromosomal regions such as centromeres.
source: The CTD is subject to extensive post-translational modifications (Antoniou-Kourounioti et al., 2019; Bedez et al., 2018; Cardenas et al., 1992; Grozav et al., 2011; Mao et al., 2000), has been shown to mediate interactions with different partner proteins (Lane et al., 2013; Nakano et al., 1996; Niimi et al., 2001; Yamane et al., 1997) and, specifically for Top2α, appears to help localize the enzyme to specialized chromosomal regions such as centromeres (Andersen et al., 2002; Pandey et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andersen et al., 2002; Pandey et al., 2020; Yoshida et al., 2016.

claim: Some proteins known to associate with topo IIs and some genetic loci where the enzyme is enriched have been proposed to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS).
source: Interestingly, some proteins known to associate with topo IIs and some genetic loci where the enzyme is enriched have been proposed to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming assemblies that distinguish them from general chromatin areas (Boija et al., 2018; Cebrián et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018; Frattini et al., 2021; Trivedi et al., 2019; Yamane et al., 1997; Zamudio et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boija et al., 2018; Cebrián et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2018; Frattini et al., 2021; Trivedi et al., 2019; Yamane et al., 1997; Zamudio et al., 2019.

claim: During LLPS, macromolecules locally concentrate to form a new fluid phase that demixes from the bulk solution to establish a dynamic, membraneless compartment.
source: During LLPS, macromolecules locally concentrate to form a new fluid phase that demixes from the bulk solution to establish a dynamic, membraneless compartment (Banani et al., 2017; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017.

claim: The CTDs of eukaryotic topo IIs are long, intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).
source: Limited proteolysis studies (Austin et al., 1995), as well as primary sequence analysis using the disordered protein prediction algorithm IUPRed2A (Erdős and Dosztányi, 2020), indicate that the CTDs of eukaryotic topo IIs are long, intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Austin et al., 1995 and Erdős and Dosztányi, 2020, and by disorder prediction data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: IDRs have been shown to facilitate the self-assembly of macromolecules into liquid-like condensates through phase separation in a variety of protein systems.
source: IDRs have been shown to facilitate the self-assembly of macromolecules into liquid-like condensates through phase separation in a variety of protein systems (Banani et al., 2017; Lyon et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017; Lyon et al., 2021.

claim: Many proteins that undergo phase separation possess IDRs that exhibit low amino acid sequence complexity.
source: Many proteins that undergo phase separation possess IDRs that exhibit low amino acid sequence complexity (Franzmann and Alberti, 2019; Uversky, 2017); exceptions include factors that support the initiation of DNA replication in metazoans, which have an IDR sequence complexity similar to that of folded proteins except for a lack of aromatic residues (Parker et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2019), and the Nephrin Intracellular Domain (NICD) (Pak et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Franzmann and Alberti, 2019; Uversky, 2017.

claim: Eukaryotic replication initiators have an IDR sequence complexity similar to that of folded proteins except for a lack of aromatic residues.
source: Many proteins that undergo phase separation possess IDRs that exhibit low amino acid sequence complexity (Franzmann and Alberti, 2019; Uversky, 2017); exceptions include factors that support the initiation of DNA replication in metazoans, which have an IDR sequence complexity similar to that of folded proteins except for a lack of aromatic residues (Parker et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2019), and the Nephrin Intracellular Domain (NICD) (Pak et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Parker et al., 2021; Parker et al., 2019.

claim: Topo II CTDs generally have a high lysine content (≥15%), a moderately high amount of serine (~10%), aspartate, and glutamate (10%), and a very low percentage of each aromatic amino acid (<5%).
source: Analysis of the relative amino-acid composition of topo II CTDs shows that despite having relatively sparse sequence homology to each other (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the elements generally have a high lysine content (≥15%), a moderately high amount of serine (~10%), aspartate, and glutamate (10%), and a very low percentage of each aromatic amino acid (<5%) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on amino acid composition analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Eukaryotic topo II CTDs can have different compositions of positively and negatively charged amino acids and varied isoelectric points (pI = 5.5–9.6).
source: Despite these similarities, eukaryotic topo II CTDs can have different compositions of positively and negatively charged amino acids and varied isoelectric points (pI = 5.5–9.6) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The compositional properties of the topo II CTDs are more similar to those of the eukaryotic replication initiators, as opposed to low-complexity sequences found in representative LLPS-forming proteins such as human FUS or DDX4.
source: Overall, the compositional properties of the topo II CTDs are more similar to those of the eukaryotic replication initiators, as opposed to low-complexity sequences found in representative LLPS-forming proteins such as human FUS (Wang et al., 2018a) or DDX4 (Nott et al., 2015; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citations to Wang et al., 2018a and Nott et al., 2015.

claim: At the lowest concentration of ScTop2 tested (50nM), no visible bodies were seen.
source: At the lowest concentration of ScTop2 tested (50nM), no visible bodies were seen.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At moderate protein concentrations (375nM), small circular fluorescent bodies became apparent.
source: However, at moderate protein concentrations (375nM), small circular fluorescent bodies became apparent.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Puncta formed by ScTop2 grew in size and number as protein concentration increased.
source: These bodies (referred to hereafter as 'puncta') grew in size and number as protein concentration increased.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The formation of puncta by ScTop2 was time-dependent, with puncta appearing within 10min of mixing and plateauing in number and size after~60min.
source: While conducting these experiments, we noted that the formation of puncta was time-dependent, with puncta appearing within 10min of mixing and plateauing in number and size after~60min (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Both ScTop2 protein and DNA co-localize in the puncta.
source: Imaging at Cy3 and Cy5 excitation wavelengths showed that both protein and DNA co-localize in the puncta; the labeled DNA on its own did not form such bodies (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on dual-channel confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DNA-dependent stimulation of puncta formation was also observed when Cy3-ScTop2 was mixed with an unlabeled negatively supercoiled 2.9kb plasmid (pSG483).
source: DNA-dependent stimulation of puncta formation was also observed when Cy3-ScTop2 was mixed with an unlabeled negatively supercoiled 2.9kb plasmid (pSG483) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Puncta formed in the presence of DNA were noticeably larger compared to those formed without.
source: Interestingly, puncta formed in the presence of DNA were noticeably larger compared to those formed without (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Budding yeast topo II can form higher-order spherical assemblies at protein concentrations greater than 250nM.
source: Collectively, these data show that budding yeast topo II can form higher-order spherical assemblies at protein concentrations greater than 250nM and that DNA both stimulates the formation of and is integrated into these bodies.
evidence: This is based on the confocal microscopy data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: DNA both stimulates the formation of and is integrated into ScTop2 bodies.
source: Collectively, these data show that budding yeast topo II can form higher-order spherical assemblies at protein concentrations greater than 250nM and that DNA both stimulates the formation of and is integrated into these bodies.
evidence: This is based on the confocal microscopy data presented in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: The shortest DNA tested (50bp) did not increase the number nor the size of condensates at any concentration tested.
source: The shortest DNA tested (50bp, roughly the binding site size of the catalytic region) did not increase the number nor the size of condensates at any concentration tested.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The 100bp, 200bp, and pSG483 DNA substrates all enhanced condensate formation at intermediate mass concentrations (5–20ng/µL).
source: By comparison, the 100bp, 200bp, and pSG483 DNA substrates all enhanced condensate formation at intermediate mass concentrations (5–20ng/µL).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Heparin failed to stimulate DNA condensation at the observed concentrations.
source: To determine whether the stimulation of condensation was dependent on DNA, a titration was also conducted with another polyanionic substrate, heparin. Interestingly, heparin failed to stimulate DNA condensation at the observed concentrations.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Condensate formation by ScTop2 is aided by extended DNA segments and is not stimulated simply by the presence of a poly-anionic substrate.
source: Together, these findings establish that condensate formation by ScTop2 is aided by extended DNA segments and is not stimulated simply by the presence of a poly-anionic substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the DNA length and heparin titration experiments.

claim: Nucleic-acid binding proteins that undergo phase separation tend to exhibit a biphasic response with respect to the relative concentration of DNA or RNA.
source: Nucleic-acid binding proteins that undergo phase separation tend to exhibit a biphasic response with respect to the relative concentration of DNA or RNA (Du and Chen, 2018; Maharana et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015): as a nucleic acid substrate is titrated against a fixed amount of protein, condensation is first promoted, but then as concentrations are increased further, the protein is solubilized and condensation is antagonized.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Du and Chen, 2018; Maharana et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: At low DNA concentrations (5–10nM), the number and size of puncta increased relative to samples in the absence of DNA.
source: At low DNA concentrations (5–10nM), the number and size of puncta increased relative to samples in the absence of DNA.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: As the DNA concentration was increased further, puncta disappeared.
source: By contrast, as the DNA concentration was increased further, puncta disappeared.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At intermediate concentrations of DNA tested (25 and 50nM), observed bodies took on elongated, fibril-like shapes for the plasmid substrate.
source: Interestingly, at the intermediate concentrations of DNA tested (25 and 50nM), observed bodies took on elongated, fibril-like shapes for the plasmid substrate (Figure 2E); by comparison, puncta formed with short DNAs remained spherical.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Puncta formed with short DNAs remained spherical.
source: Interestingly, at the intermediate concentrations of DNA tested (25 and 50nM), observed bodies took on elongated, fibril-like shapes for the plasmid substrate (Figure 2E); by comparison, puncta formed with short DNAs remained spherical.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations.

claim: This size-dependent type of behavior has been previously seen with other DNA-binding proteins that undergo LLPS, such as HP1α.
source: This size-dependent type of behavior has been previously seen with other DNA-binding proteins that undergo LLPS, such as HP1α (Keenen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Keenen et al., 2021.

claim: In reactions lacking DNA, the intensity of the Cy3-ScTop2 puncta did not recover following photobleaching, suggesting that these bodies possess more gel-like characteristics.
source: In reactions lacking DNA, the intensity of the Cy3-ScTop2 puncta did not recover following photobleaching, suggesting that these bodies possess more gel-like characteristics (Frey et al., 2006; Jawerth et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on FRAP data shown in Figure 3B and citations to Frey et al., 2006; Jawerth et al., 2020.

claim: In the presence of 5nM unlabeled pSG483, a fraction of the Cy3-ScTop2 intensity (roughly one-third) had recovered by the 15 minute mark.
source: By contrast, in the presence of 5nM unlabeled pSG483, a fraction of the Cy3-ScTop2 intensity (roughly one-third) had recovered by the same 15minute mark.
evidence: This is based on FRAP data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: As the pSG483 concentration increased, the mobile protein fraction inside the puncta appeared to decrease.
source: As the pSG483 concentration increased, the mobile protein fraction inside the puncta appeared to decrease, with the fibrillar bodies (25–50nM DNA) showing somewhat less fluidity than the spherical droplets (5–10nM DNA).
evidence: This is based on FRAP data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Time-lapse microscopy of puncta containing ScTop2 and 5nM pSG483 revealed fusion events between puncta on the order of minutes.
source: Time-lapse microscopy of puncta containing ScTop2 and 5nM pSG483 also revealed fusion events between puncta on the order of minutes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: While the smaller puncta formed by ScTop2 on its own are relatively static, the protein in both the spherical and fibrillar structures formed by ScTop2 in the presence of DNA is dynamic, exhibiting the defining attributes of condensates formed by LLPS.
source: Thus, while the smaller puncta formed by ScTop2 on its own are relatively static, the protein in both the spherical and fibrillar structures formed by ScTop2 in the presence of DNA is dynamic, exhibiting the defining attributes of condensates formed by LLPS.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP and fusion data.

claim: The Cy3-ScTop2ΔCTD construct did not form condensates in either the presence or absence of a 200bp Cy5-labeled DNA, even at protein concentrations as high as 1μM.
source: The Cy3-ScTop2ΔCTD construct did not form condensates in either the presence or absence of a 200bp Cy5-labeled DNA, even at protein concentrations as high as 1μM.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The Cy3-labeled CTD failed to form condensates in the absence of DNA but did form bodies in the presence of 50nM Cy5-labeled 200bp duplex at a lower salt concentration of 50mM KOAc.
source: By comparison, the Cy3-labeled CTD failed to form condensates in the absence of DNA but did form bodies in the presence of 50nM Cy5-labeled 200bp duplex at a lower salt concentration of 50mM KOAc (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Several puncta formed with the CTD alone integrated DNA into only a portion of the bodies, as compared to the fully homogenous distribution of DNA seen with full-length ScTop2.
source: Interestingly, several puncta formed with the CTD alone integrated DNA into only a portion of the bodies, as compared to the fully homogenous distribution of DNA seen with full-length ScTop2 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The addition of PEG as a crowding agent induced puncta formation by the CTD, but in a manner that did not require DNA.
source: The addition of PEG as a crowding agent also induced puncta formation by the CTD, but in a manner that did not require DNA, indicating that this region can weakly associate with itself (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ScTop2 CTD is necessary for supporting LLPS by the full-length enzyme.
source: Overall, these findings demonstrate that the ScTop2 CTD is necessary for supporting LLPS by the full-length enzyme and that DNA can act as a scaffold to promote co-localization of the element.
evidence: This is inferred from the deletion and isolated CTD experiments.

claim: DNA can act as a scaffold to promote co-localization of the CTD element.
source: Overall, these findings demonstrate that the ScTop2 CTD is necessary for supporting LLPS by the full-length enzyme and that DNA can act as a scaffold to promote co-localization of the element.
evidence: This is inferred from the CTD experiments with DNA.

claim: In the absence of DNA, the small puncta formed by ScTop2 alone at the control potassium acetate concentration (150mM) disappeared as soon as salt levels were increased to 200mM.
source: In the absence of DNA, the small puncta formed by ScTop2 alone at the control potassium acetate concentration (150mM) disappeared as soon as salt levels were increased to 200mM.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the presence of pSG483, the large condensates seen at 150mM salt persisted until potassium acetate levels reached 400mM.
source: By comparison, in the presence of pSG483, the large condensates seen at 150mM salt persisted until potassium acetate levels reached 400mM.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The intermediate salt concentrations still supported solubilization of ScTop2 condensates by elevated levels of plasmid DNA.
source: Interestingly, the intermediate salt concentrations still supported solubilization of ScTop2 condensates by elevated levels of plasmid DNA.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol strongly promoted the aggregation of ScTop2 into large, irregular bodies in both the presence and absence of DNA while also preventing the resolubilization of the bodies when pSG483 concentrations were increased.
source: Interestingly, 1,6-HD strongly promoted the aggregation of ScTop2 into large, irregular bodies in both the presence and absence of DNA while also preventing the resolubilization of the bodies when pSG483 concentrations were increased.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The addition of higher levels of 1,6-HD (e.g. 10%) severely disrupted DNA supercoil relaxation by ScTop2.
source: The addition of higher levels of 1,6-HD (e.g. 10%) also severely disrupted DNA supercoil relaxation by ScTop2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), indicating that the agent has a detrimental effect on the protein.
evidence: This is based on activity assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The CTD was unable to form condensates in the absence of DNA, even when the salt concentration was lowered to 50mM potassium acetate.
source: As seen previously, the CTD was unable to form condensates in the absence of DNA, even when the salt concentration was lowered to 50mM potassium acetate (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Robust CTD-DNA interactions were seen at 50mM salt concentration, as evidenced by the presence of large numbers of large puncta and by the co-localization of DNA inside the CTD bodies.
source: However, robust CTD-DNA interactions were seen at this lower salt concentration, as evidenced not only by the presence of large numbers of large puncta, but also by the co-localization of DNA inside the CTD bodies; as salt concentration was increased, puncta became more diffuse.
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: As salt concentration was increased, puncta formed by the CTD became more diffuse.

source: The type IIA topoisomerase cleavage core binds 20–30bp of DNA (Dong and Berger, 2007; Lee et al., 1989; Peng and Marians, 1995; Thomsen et al., 1990); given that larger DNA substrates are needed to promote LLPS (≥100bp) (Figure 2E), it is likely that DNA acts as a bridge to enhance condensation for native topo II as it does with the CTD alone.

claim: At low (1–10nM) protein concentrations in vitro, eukaryotic topo II will generate steady-state distributions of DNA products roughly in accord with thermodynamic expectations for the concentration of DNA used in the reaction.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Rybenkov et al., 1997.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Padget et al., 2000 and Hsieh, 1983.

claim: DNA catenation with low levels of topo II can be induced in vitro by the addition of proteinaceous or chemical DNA condensing agents, which increase the close proximity of DNA strands to favor linking.
source: DNA catenation with low levels of topo II can be induced in vitro by the addition of proteinaceous (Riou et al., 1985; Tse et al., 1984) or chemical (Krasnow and Cozzarelli, 1982) DNA condensing agents, which increase the close proximity of DNA strands to favor linking; the ability of moderate concentrations of enzyme to do the same implies that topo II can directly condense DNA strands, a concept validated here.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Riou et al., 1985; Tse et al., 1984; Krasnow and Cozzarelli, 1982.

claim: The ability of moderate concentrations of enzyme to induce catenation implies that topo II can directly condense DNA strands.
source: DNA catenation with low levels of topo II can be induced in vitro by the addition of proteinaceous (Riou et al., 1985; Tse et al., 1984) or chemical (Krasnow and Cozzarelli, 1982) DNA condensing agents, which increase the close proximity of DNA strands to favor linking; the ability of moderate concentrations of enzyme to do the same implies that topo II can directly condense DNA strands, a concept validated here.

source: A likely factor contributing to the ability of type II topoisomerases that lack an IDR to form knots, such as T4 topo II or ScTop2∆CTD, is the sharp DNA bend introduced by the cleavage region of the enzyme (Dong and Berger, 2007; Vologodskii et al., 2001; Figure 7A).

source: At low protein concentrations, any given plasmid should have only a few enzymes bound at a time, which favors the binding and resolution of crossovers already present in the substrate, such as those arising from plectonemic supercoils (the affinity of topo II for supercoiled DNA is at least 10 fold greater than for relaxed substrates [Osheroff, 1986; Osheroff, 1987; Zechiedrich and Osheroff, 1990]).
